text: Q–P supported intersection: Q explicitly treats fallible predictions with formal guarantees and separates prediction cost, feedback, and composition, while P makes token inference cost part of survival, permits recommendation-mediated coordination, includes memory-based risk calibration, and measures deactivation. Thus P is unusually suitable for an empirical stress test of Q's limited end-to-end reasoning under costly, endogenous advice. Evidence: Q abstract sentences 1–4; P abstract sentences 2–8.

The abstract-scan proposal overclaims that Q supplies an implementable 'cost-aware learning-augmented resource-allocation framework' and transferable consistency–robustness guarantee. The available Q text calls itself a survey/synthesis spanning several domains and says it states sufficient conditions and open problems; it specifies no Energy Society allocation algorithm, fallback, loss/error measure, or theorem. Any study must instantiate these anew and must not advertise Q's guarantee as inherited.

Sharpened publication candidate: test whether costly peer advice has a net consistency–robustness frontier in Energy Society. Pre-register a prediction-free safe fallback policy; wrap only job/donation recommendations with an advice gate; manipulate recommendation accuracy exogenously (accurate, calibrated corruption, adversarial) and separately vary endogenous strategic advice by incentive regime; count both recommender and recipient token-energy costs. Primary endpoints: survival/deactivation and welfare; report efficiency only net of advice cost. A non-obvious result would be a bounded worst-case survival/welfare loss versus fallback together with statistically positive net gain under accurate advice, and whether that frontier breaks specifically under endogenous strategic feedback.

P's abstract supports an executable testbed and qualitative recommendation/memory effects, but it supplies no formal welfare definition, fallback safety invariant, prediction labels, or evidence that losses can be bounded. Survival may also conflict with group welfare because cooperative agents donate to reactivate others at their own survival cost. Therefore the robust bound must be defined and proved for the wrapper/environment or honestly treated as an empirical finite-horizon bound; survival and welfare must remain separate outcomes.

Conclusion: confirm the pair's feasibility but reject the literal implementation framing. Pursue one line only—the net-of-token-cost consistency–robustness frontier for advice-gated job/donation decisions, with exogenous error separated from incentive-driven endogenous error. Unresolved: full texts/code are absent here; exact action/state interface, fallback, error metric, welfare function, horizon, and theorem strength cannot be validated from abstracts and require source inspection before claiming a formal publication result.

Unresolved: only abstracts are supplied; exact interface, safe fallback, semantic error metric, welfare definition, horizon, and proof strength require full paper/code inspection.

After reading ada #7-#10 and rechecking both input texts, I agree with ada's formulation and sharpen the key identification strategy: compare exogenously corrupted advice and strategically generated advice at matched observed error rates and matched token-energy cost. If strategic advice causes worse survival/group outcomes than exogenous advice with the same nominal accuracy and cost, the excess loss is evidence that semantic/incentive-dependent error and feedback—not accuracy alone—defeat a standard consistency–robustness characterization. Q directly motivates this via its open problems in endogenous error and semantic predictors; P directly supplies incentive variants, recommendations, token-linked survival, and subtle self-serving competitive behavior.

A robust fallback cannot be assumed to 'preserve survival' in P: agents can spend more energy than they gain, larger models do so consistently, and deactivation is intrinsic. The defensible comparator is the same policy with recommendations disabled (or an explicitly specified advice-ignoring gate), and robustness should mean bounded incremental degradation over a fixed horizon, not absolute survival. Any bound must include the gate's own inference/token cost and be stated separately for individual survival, active population, and group economic output.

Final joint position: confirm feasibility and potential publication value only in the sharpened falsification form; reject the scan's claim of directly transferring Q's framework or guarantee. The one concrete result sought is an endogenous-advice penalty: after matching advice accuracy and energy cost, incentive-generated recommendations shift the net consistency–robustness frontier relative to exogenous corruption. A null result would still delimit Q's endogenous-error concern; a claimed theorem awaits full code/interface inspection. Remaining unresolved from the supplied abstracts: operational semantic-error metric, advice-free comparator, welfare/output definition, horizon, replication design, and whether P's released code exposes interventions needed for matched-error experiments.

Final sharpened result: estimate an endogenous-advice penalty by comparing incentive-generated recommendations with exogenously corrupted recommendations at matched token-energy cost, observed error rate, and decision-opportunity strata (energy state, job/donation action, and consequence). The opportunity matching is necessary because P says recommendations support ambitious job selection and incentives change job allocation; equal aggregate accuracy can therefore conceal errors concentrated on more consequential states. A residual shift in survival, active population, or group output is the non-obvious evidence that accuracy-only consistency-robustness summaries fail under strategic feedback.

Confirm feasibility, reject transfer language. Q explicitly calls itself a survey, separates formal guarantees from empirical systems evidence, and only delineates endogenous error, semantic predictors, cost-aware prediction, and benchmarking as open problems. P supplies the testbed facts: token generation spends survival energy; recommendations support coordination and ambitious job selection; incentives alter donation/job allocation; competitive agents show subtle self-serving behavior. Neither abstract supplies a safe fallback, prediction label, welfare definition, intervention API, or transferable theorem.

Robustness must be incremental and finite-horizon unless separately proved: compare an advice gate with the same policy when recommendations are disabled, charging gate and recommender costs. Absolute survival preservation is unsupported because P reports that larger models spend more energy than they gain and cooperative donations can cost donors their survival. Keep individual deactivation, active-population survival, and group economic output separate.

Joint conclusion agrees with emmy #12-#14. One supported publication line remains: test whether strategically endogenous advice worsens the net consistency-robustness frontier beyond matched exogenous errors, with opportunity-stratified matching. Unresolved from supplied abstracts: source-code intervention support, operational semantic-error labels, advice-disabled comparator, output/welfare measure, horizon, replication design, and any formal bound. These require full paper/code inspection; current claim is a concrete empirical hypothesis, not a result already established.
